newsitem.title: ISRAEL: No progress in Israel, PLO talks as Ross heads home.
newsitem.headline: No progress in Israel, PLO talks as Ross heads home.

text.p: U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross said before heading home on Friday there was a "very clear desire" to break the deadlock in Israeli-Palestinian peace talks.

"I think what is important as I leave the region is that there is a very clear desire to find a way out... to find a way to promote moving towards peace," Ross said after a two-hour meeting with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
Ross held talks with Arafat in the West Bank town of Nablus shortly after meeting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Jerusalem, Israeli media reported.
Palestinian officials said Arafat, who had declined to meet Ross on Thursday, told the American envoy he wanted the U.S. to take a more active role in mediation.
"Arafat told Ross that a greater American role is the only way out of the crisis," said Arafat adviser Nabil Abu Rdainah.
Ross, on his second shuttle mission in a month, failed to thaw a two-month-old freeze in peace talks, sparked by Israel's groundbreaking on a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
"I will be reporting back to the president (Bill Clinton) and the secretary (Madeleine Albright) on how to best work with the parties to move ahead and to try to proceed," Ross said.
"We will continue to be facilitating contact between the parties because we know the best way to move forward is for all of us to work together," he added.
The Palestinians demand Israel halt settlement activity, which it views as pre-empting final peace talks, as a condition for resuming negotiations.
Israel, accusing the Palestinian Authority of creating an "artificial crisis" in negotiations has linked a resumption of talks with a PLO crackdown on "terror".
"There is an attempt, apparently, by the Palestinan Authority, by its leader, to create an artificial crisis," said Israeli Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh earlier on Friday.
Arafat sent a letter to Clinton complaining indirectly at Ross's performance and asking Clinton to personally step in to salvage the process, Abu Rdainah said.

"Arafat informed Ross that he is not happy with the American mediation role and the Israeli delaying tactics. That is why he sent the letter to President Clinton asking him to intervene personally to resolve the crisis," Abu Rdainah said.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright told visiting Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy that it could provide only limited help to move the process forward.
Albright also made it clear that she was not prepared to visit the region until the parties made "difficult decisions" required to overcome the current impasse.
